name: The Metric
kick: gravity & geometry · first principles · how you measure distance and time at each point
title: The metric — the measuring rule that makes geometry work
lede: A curved surface has no outside ruler laid over it. How do you measure distances between nearby points when you cannot step outside the surface itself? Equip each point with a local measuring rule — the metric — that says how many kilometers a tiny step in each direction costs. Add up these costs along any path and you get its length. From this one object alone — knowing the metric everywhere — every other geometric fact follows: straightest paths, curvature, even the passage of time in relativity. Here is the idea, why it is the master object, what it reveals on a real run, where it breaks, and the surprise where time itself is measured by the same rule.
arc: Why the metric is the master

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — how to measure distances on a curved surface from within

blocks.html: Imagine you are a flatlander living on the surface of a sphere — say, the Earth. You have never left that surface. A ruler, to you, is a string laid along the surface. When you ask 'how far is New York to London?' you need a real answer: lay a string from one city to the other and measure its length. But which string? You could curve it lazily around the globe the long way, or pull it tight. Only the tight one gives a genuine distance — the shortest path between two points. But what makes that path 'the tightest'?

That is the deep question. A curved surface has no outside ruler pressed against it from above. You cannot judge 'how curved' a small region is, or 'which is the straightest path,' unless you have a way to measure distance and angle from within the surface itself. You need a rule at each point that says: if I take a tiny step this direction, how many kilometers does that cost?

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — the metric: the measuring rule that lives at each point

blocks.html: The solution is to equip each point of the surface with a metric — a measuring rule encoded as a rule for distances. At any point, the metric tells you: if you move by a tiny amount in the north direction and a tiny amount in the east direction, what is the total distance you traveled? On a flat sheet the answer is simple — the Pythagorean theorem — but on a curved surface the metric must bend to fit the shape. On Earth, near the North Pole, a step east is much shorter than a step east at the equator, because the circles of constant latitude get smaller. The metric captures that.

Once you know the metric everywhere, everything else flows from it. To find the longest distance between two cities, you integrate — add up infinitely many tiny costs along any path. The shortest such path is the geodesic, what we call 'the straightest path on a curved surface.' Curvature itself can be read off from the metric, no outside observer needed. In relativity, the metric also measures time — it tells you how fast time passes at different points and in different states of motion. The geometry and the physics are one object.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — the metric on a globe computes New York to London

blocks.html: We computed the distance from New York to London using the metric embedded in the Earth's surface — the rule that converts tiny coordinate steps (latitude and longitude) into real kilometers. The metric says: a step north is always about 111 km per degree, but a step east depends on your latitude. The computation follows the shortest path — the great circle — all the way from one city to the other. No outside ruler was used; only the surface's own measuring rule.

blocks.caption: The great circle is longer than the flat-map line because it curves to follow the sphere. The metric, applied along the curve, tells you the actual kilometers traveled on Earth's surface.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: the metric on Earth's surface converts tiny coordinate steps into kilometers, and when you sum those costs along the great-circle arc, you get the true distance of 5567 km. The metric is not drawn from outside; it lives in the surface itself. This is what separates genuine distance from coordinate illusion. Any other coordinate system on Earth — longitude and latitude shifted, or measured in degrees per meter — would compute the same 5567 km, because the underlying geometry is coordinate-free.

sections.h2: 4 · Why the metric is the master object

blocks.html: The metric is the master because geometry follows from it alone. Once you specify how to measure distances everywhere, the straightest paths are determined: they are the ones that feel locally straight at every step, yet pile up to be the shortest global distance. Curvature is determined: the stronger the metric twists between nearby points, the higher the curvature. Angles and areas are determined: measure with the metric and you know them. Free-falling bodies and light rays in spacetime move along geodesics — the metric's straightest paths — which is why gravity is not a force but a shape. Einstein's whole theory is an equation for the metric: matter and energy warp the metric, and the warped metric tells all objects and light rays how to move.

The metric is also the cleanest way to separate real geometry from illusion. The same sphere can be described using infinitely many different coordinate grids — longitude and latitude, or Mercator projection, or polar coordinates from a chosen pole. The coordinates change, but the metric transforms with them in a precise way, so the geometry stays the same. This means: a fact about distances or angles that is stated in terms of the metric is genuine and absolute. A fact that depends on your choice of coordinates is illusion.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real limit — the metric is defined only up to your coordinate choice

blocks.html: Here lies the deepest subtlety: the metric is not uniquely defined. The same geometry can be written down using different coordinate systems, each with its own metric formula. The sphere on Earth uses one metric in longitude and latitude, a different metric in Cartesian coordinates, another in polar coordinates. The geometry is identical, but the metric looks different in each coordinate system. So the metric alone is not the invariant object — what is invariant is the set of distances and angles the metric generates, independent of coordinates used. A careless reader might think a change in coordinates breaks the geometry. It does not; the metric transforms carefully to preserve all measured distances. You must separate the genuine geometry (which is coordinate-free) from the metric formula (which changes with coordinates). This is why the subject can feel slippery: the words 'metric' and 'coordinates' get tangled.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — in relativity the metric measures time as well as space, and gravity is its shape

blocks.html: At first, 'metric' sounds like a tool for measuring space only. But Einstein's radical move was to put space and time on equal footing in a single metric. The metric in spacetime tells you: if I move by a tiny amount in space and a tiny amount in time, what is the combined 'distance' between two events in spacetime? This 'distance' is called the interval, and it is not the everyday sum of spatial distance and time elapsed. Instead, the metric mixes them: depending on how fast you are moving and how strong gravity is, the balance between space and time in the metric changes. A fast-moving clock ticks slower — the metric says time costs less; a clock higher in a gravitational field ticks faster — the metric says time costs more. A light ray always travels along paths where the spacetime interval is zero, which is why light cannot be slowed below its speed.

Einstein's equation is an equation for the metric: matter and energy on one side, the curvature of the metric on the other. Gravity is nothing but the shape of this measuring rule, bent by the presence of mass. Trace the curvature of the metric and you have traced gravity. This is why gravity is not a force (which would be added to the other forces), but a geometry — the metric, the master object, warped.

recipe.summary: Compute the great-circle distance from New York to London on Earth using the metric embedded in spherical coordinates (latitude, longitude). The metric converts tiny latitude and longitude steps into kilometers; integrate along the geodesic to get the path length. Compare to the flat-map distance to show the curve. numpy, SI units, Earth radius R = 6.371 million meters.
recipe.eq:
metric on a sphere: ds^2 = R^2 (dθ^2 + sin^2(θ) dφ^2)
  where θ = latitude, φ = longitude, R = Earth radius
integrate ds along the great circle from New York to London
geodesic distance = 5567 km (the integral's output)
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/gr_run.py (EXP2). The 5567 km number is the run's output verbatim. The metric rule is applied without any outside ruler or coordinate system imposed from above — only the surface's own measuring rule.
